title: Holding the breath
hook: he tries stopping the breath; his head roars like a blacksmith's bellows (MN 36)

segments.voice: Yesterday, five companions: Kondañña and four others, who joined him near Uruvela. Your line was you don't go alone. Who did you tell? Day forty-four.

Try to fall asleep by force. Squeeze your eyes shut. Command yourself: sleep, now. It never works, does it? The harder you push, the more awake you get. Some things in life just don't respond to force. The wanderer has left his two teachers, and he's decided to try the other great method of his time: the hard way. Many ascetics in India believed that if you pushed the body hard enough, through pain, hunger, stillness, the mind would break through. So he pushes. He clenches his teeth, presses his tongue to the roof of his mouth, and tries to crush his thoughts by sheer will. Sweat pours from his armpits. And then he tries something harder. Today, holding the breath.
screen: `SLEEP BY FORCE NEVER WORKS.` → `THE HARD WAY.` → `CRUSHING THOUGHT BY WILL.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells this himself, years later, to a man named Saccaka. He describes what he called the breathless meditation. He stopped breathing through his mouth and nose. And when he did, he says, there was a loud roaring of winds coming out of his ears, like the roar of a blacksmith's bellows. He kept going. He stopped the breath in his ears too. And then, he says, it felt like a strong man was splitting his head with a sharp sword. Then like a tight leather strap being wound around his head. Then like a butcher carving up his belly. Then like his whole body was being roasted over hot coals. It's a hard passage to hear, and he tells it plainly. Here's the part people remember. Through all of it, he says, his energy was strong and his mindfulness was steady. He wasn't weak. He wasn't lazy. He did it as hard as a person can do it. And yet, the painful feeling didn't take hold of his mind in a way that freed it. It just hurt. He was forcing, and forcing wasn't finding. This is why, to this day, Buddhist meditation teachers say something that surprises beginners: don't control the breath. Let it breathe itself. The practice he would later teach, mindfulness of breathing, is almost the opposite of this story. You don't hold the breath. You watch it, and let it be long when it's long and short when it's short.
screen: `TOLD TO SACCAKA.` · `WINDS ROARING LIKE A BELLOWS.` · `STRONG EFFORT, NO FREEDOM.` · `LET THE BREATH BREATHE ITSELF.` · then, large: `FORCING ISN'T FINDING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Take three long, easy breaths. Don't push them. Just let each one be a little slower than the last, the way a swing slows down on its own. In, and out. In, and out. In, and out. Then stop managing it altogether. Let the breath do what it wants. Long or short, deep or shallow. Your only job is to notice it. If you catch yourself controlling it, smile, and let go again. The bell holds the time.
Holding the breath. The breathless meditation the wanderer forced himself through, and learned from: strong effort, great pain, no freedom.
Your line: forcing isn't finding. Today, when something won't work, a lid, a problem, a conversation, stop pushing for one breath, and see what changes. Day forty-four.

howItsDone: In Buddhist breath meditation (anapanasati), practitioners are taught not to hold or control the breath but to know it as it is, long or short, and teachers often cite the Buddha's austerities as the path he rejected.

fork.setup: you've stopped the breath and your ears roar like a bellows. your will is strong. what do you do?
options: push harder: stop the breath in the ears too.
fork.reveal: he pushes harder, and the pain gets worse: a sword, a strap, a butcher's knife, hot coals. it hurts, but it doesn't free him.

original.note: Pali: breathless; the appāṇaka jhāna, the breathless meditation of MN 36.

trapdoor: what you thought: holding your breath is a meditation technique.
what it means: the Buddha tried it, as hard as a person can, and found that forcing isn't finding.

what a scholar hears: MN 36 (Mahasaccaka Sutta) describes the appāṇaka jhāna and its pains, and says the painful feeling did not invade his mind; the later anapanasati teaching lets the breath be as it is.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the breathless meditation
Anapanasati Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 118): knowing a long breath as long, a short breath as short

notes: MN 36 paraphrased: teeth clenched, tongue pressed to palate; breathless meditation; bellows, sword, strap, butcher, coals. Confirm the order of similes.

Key line interpreted: MN 36 says the painful feeling 'did not invade my mind and remain'. The script says it 'didn't take hold of his mind in a way that freed it', meaning austerity didn't bring awakening. A Keeper should check this reading carefully.
Tomorrow (45) covers fasting; day 46 covers the gods thinking he'd died; both omitted here.
